hardware.headline: A machine is more than a list of pins.
hardware.body: Switches, lamps and coils need different behaviour. Bring their configuration together while keeping the limits for high-current outputs close to the hardware they protect.

sections.title: Switches and buttons
sections.text: Configure playfield switches, cabinet buttons and other digital inputs. The ESP handles input debouncing.

sections.title: LEDs and RGB strips
sections.text: Control individual LEDs and addressable RGB strips. Use them with the lighting tools to create effects and scenes.

sections.title: Coils and solenoids
sections.text: Configure flippers, bumpers and other coil-driven mechanisms with supported pulse and hold modes and built-in safety limits.

sections.title: Sensors and displays
sections.text: Connect supported accelerometers for movement and tilt detection, and supported I²C character displays.

sections.title: Find and organise your connections
sections.text: Use Reload Pins to refresh the available hardware pins from your connected ESP32-S3, including supported expansion hardware where discovery is available. Assign friendly names and functions so you can refer to your components throughout Pinball CTL without having to remember pin numbers.
items: Functions and drivers in one table

sections.title: Configure once, use across your game
sections.text: Your hardware mapping is used by the rule editor, lighting tools and other parts of Pinball CTL. Save your configuration and sync supported settings to the ESP32-S3 when you're ready to test your machine.

sections.title: Hardware safety
sections.text: Configure safe pin states and appropriate output limits for your hardware. Coil control includes configurable pulse, hold and cooldown settings, with safety limits enforced by the ESP32-S3.
items: The ESP enforces configured coil pulse and hold limits, cooldowns, arming requirements and watchdogs. Configure limits for your actual coils and drivers.
Use pulse outputs, PWM hold or paired windings where supported. New coil configurations begin disabled with conservative defaults.

steps.title: Map
steps.text: Identify the connected pins and give each component a useful name.

steps.title: Configure
steps.text: Choose the output driver and appropriate limits for the actual hardware.

steps.title: Deploy
steps.text: Save and sync the mapping, then validate the real machine deliberately.

example.title: Start with one output
example.text: A single mapped switch and correctly configured output give you a small, understandable first test before you expand the machine.

esp-connection.headline: Know which controller you are talking to.
esp-connection.body: ESPLink brings device identity, bridge status and installed firmware into the same workspace. It is a practical checkpoint between authoring a change and testing it on your machine.

sections.title: Check the controller
sections.text: View connection state, device information and firmware details from ESPLink.

sections.title: Manage the bridge
sections.text: Access connection and runtime utilities without leaving the browser.

sections.title: Prepare for updates
sections.text: Use compatibility checks and the supported local firmware apply workflow before changing controller software.

steps.title: Connect
steps.text: Attach the ESP with a data-capable USB cable.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: Review the detected device and bridge state.

steps.title: Investigate
steps.text: Use the relevant connection tools and logs if status is unexpected.

example.title: After a cable reconnect
example.text: Check that the controller identity and firmware appear again before trying a configuration sync. A running bridge alone is not the whole connection story.

firmware.headline: A clearer path from release to controller.
firmware.body: Review version information before downloading a firmware image. The local library shows which releases are ready to apply, while ESPLink handles the connected device.

sections.title: Review available versions
sections.text: Browse firmware versions and release information before choosing what to use.

sections.title: Manage release sources
sections.text: Use the default firmware feed or a supported custom source when appropriate.

sections.title: Prepare an update
sections.text: Download a selected version for use with the ESPLink firmware workflow.

steps.title: Review
steps.text: Browse version details and choose the release appropriate to your app.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.text: Download the selected version to the local firmware library.

steps.title: Apply
steps.text: Open ESPLink and follow the controller update workflow.

example.title: Working with a custom build
example.text: A custom manifest source lets you browse your own published firmware versions through the same version-management interface.

accelerometer.headline: Make motion visible.
accelerometer.body: With a supported sensor connected, the motion view brings table orientation and activity into the browser. Without one, the module clearly reports that the sensor is unavailable instead of presenting readings as live.

sections.title: Set a level baseline
sections.text: Calibrate a supported motion sensor to match its position in your cabinet.
items: Pitch and roll relative to a baseline

sections.title: Check table orientation
sections.text: View pitch and roll to help level the machine.

sections.title: Watch motion activity
sections.text: Inspect live sensor readings and nudge or lift activity from the browser.

sections.title: Use movement to control your game
sections.text: The accelerometer does more than monitor your machine's movement. It can detect nudges and when the table is lifted, generating events that you can use in your game rules. This means you can decide how your machine responds when a player moves or tilts the table.

sections.title: Create your own tilt rules
sections.text: Use the Rules editor to respond to accelerometer events. For example, you could:
items: Play a warning sound when a player nudges the machine.
Show a warning or animation on the backglass.
Apply a score penalty or track repeated nudges.
Trigger custom lighting effects or game events.
sections.after_text: These are examples of rules you can create, rather than fixed responses built into the accelerometer.

sections.title: Configure how movement is detected
sections.text: Adjust the sensitivity of nudge detection, set the angle used to detect a lifted table and configure the cooldown between events. You can also calibrate the sensor to match its mounting position and use the live readings to check how your machine responds.

sections.title: Build the behaviour you want
sections.text: Whether you want traditional pinball tilt behaviour or something specific to your own game, Pinball CTL gives you the movement events to build on. You decide what happens next.

steps.title: Connect
steps.text: Use a supported sensor and the wiring appropriate to your controller.

steps.title: Calibrate
steps.text: Set the baseline when the machine is physically level.

steps.title: Observe
steps.text: Review motion activity and verify the behaviour of your configured rules.

example.title: Revisit the mounting
example.text: After moving or remounting a sensor, check the baseline and orientation before relying on motion events in gameplay.

rule-editor.headline: Keep the logic readable as it grows.
rule-editor.body: A right-side rule settings panel shows metadata, triggers, conditions, actions and summary in dedicated tabs. Work on one part of the behaviour without losing the rest of its context.

sections.title: Choose a trigger
sections.text: Start rules from supported hardware, system or custom events.

sections.title: Add conditions
sections.text: Use flags, counters, elapsed time and supported device states to decide when a rule applies.

sections.title: Choose actions
sections.text: Configure supported actions such as emitting events and changing flags or counters.
items: Saved configuration and ESP sync status

sections.title: Turn a hit into a reason to play again.
sections.text: Rules decide what happens; scoring gives that moment value. Combine them to build a game that reacts clearly, rewards the right shots and grows beyond isolated switches.

steps.title: Describe
steps.text: Name the behaviour and add notes or tags.

steps.title: Compose
steps.text: Build its triggers, conditions and supported actions.

steps.title: Review
steps.text: Check the rule before saving, syncing and testing.

example.title: A rule you can revisit
example.text: “Left lane bonus” is easier to maintain when its timing, qualification and reward are expressed separately rather than hidden in an unexplained event name.

scoring.headline: Start with points. Build toward a game.
scoring.body: Give ordinary switch hits a baseline reward, then add hit-based rules and combinations as the play experience develops. Scoring is authored on the Pi alongside the other game tools.

sections.title: Set base points
sections.text: Assign points to the events and shots in your game.

sections.title: Create scoring rules
sections.text: Build more advanced awards, including progressive hit values where supported.

sections.title: Add combos
sections.text: Reward sequences of shots with combinations and multipliers.

sections.title: Connect rules to scoring
sections.text: Trigger points, lighting and other supported responses from the same rule workflow.

steps.title: Start simple
steps.text: Assign base points to the inputs you already have.

steps.title: Layer rewards
steps.text: Add progressive rules and combinations.

steps.title: Connect feedback
steps.text: Use emitted events to coordinate light, sound or media responses.

example.title: Make a bumper rally meaningful
example.text: A run of hits can contribute more than isolated fixed awards. Tune the scoring rule to reward sustained play, then check how it behaves during real bursts.

lighting.headline: Design light in the shape of your machine.
lighting.body: A light show makes more sense when you can see where the fixtures are. Work on the playfield stage with scene settings alongside the preview. Browse scenes in a side panel, configure fixtures from a clear table, and target the intended lights as you move from simple feedback to layered scenes.

sections.title: Arrange your fixtures
sections.text: Set up lighting fixtures, position them on the stage and organise how they appear on your playfield.

sections.title: Build and preview scenes
sections.text: Use patterns, layers and a custom timeline to create effects, then preview the result before syncing.

sections.title: Control lighting at runtime
sections.text: Use the Runtime view to inspect and test supported lighting behaviour on your connected setup.

steps.title: Arrange
steps.text: Check fixture placement and select the intended cast.

steps.title: Compose
steps.text: Choose patterns or edit frames and timeline markers.

steps.title: Deploy
steps.text: Save, compile and sync before validating the physical result.

example.title: Attract mode meets a bonus
example.text: A background scene can provide the cabinet’s atmosphere while a higher-priority response marks a game event. The blend mode determines how those layers interact.

audio.headline: Keep sounds organised and playback intentional.
audio.body: Start with a library of reusable assets. Cues describe how each sound should behave, while output and usage views help you understand where it goes and what uses it.

sections.title: Sound library
sections.text: Upload, name and preview audio files so you can find and reuse them throughout your game.
items: Return to the library with context

sections.title: Audio cues
sections.text: Create cues that your rules can trigger, and configure how playback behaves when another event occurs.

sections.title: Outputs and routing
sections.text: Choose which configured audio outputs play each cue, so you can plan sound for your cabinet.

sections.title: Audio usage
sections.text: Use the Audio Usage Map to see where sounds are referenced across your project.

steps.title: Upload
steps.text: Add and name your sound assets.

steps.title: Configure
steps.text: Create cues with the intended playback behaviour.

steps.title: Trace
steps.text: Review outputs and usage when investigating a missing or repeated sound.

example.title: Separate voice from the background
example.text: Music, voice and effects have different jobs. Named buses and cues make those intentions visible while you design the sound of a mode.

media.headline: Compose a scene, not a pile of files.
media.body: Bring text, images, video and Godot content together in a spacious preview with a compact layer stack alongside it. Select a layer to highlight it, drag to reorder, and open its sliders settings when you need more detail. Keep the library separate from the composition so assets can be reused as the game grows.

sections.title: Build display scenes
sections.text: Combine visual layers, including text, images, video and supported Godot content, to create scenes for your game.
items: Text and visuals in one authoring environment

sections.title: Media library and fonts
sections.text: Organise the files and fonts used by your scenes.

sections.title: Displays and startup content
sections.text: Choose which displays receive each scene and configure the content shown when your machine starts.

sections.title: Godot integration
sections.text: Create animated backglass scenes, menus and score displays in Godot, export a scene pack and use it in Pinball CTL's Media workflow.
items: Develop and test the scene in Godot.
Load the pack, choose its scene and configure input mappings.
sections.after_text: Build and test your content in Godot, then import its exported scene pack. The bundled backglass includes a seven-shot cinematic attract sequence, a quest menu, a fast spinning bonus tally, animated award bursts and a preview theatre for testing without cabinet hardware. All 25 screens can be installed as individual Media scenes with flipper and Select navigation. A Godot menu can respond to cabinet inputs while remaining testable with keyboard actions during development. The guide explains the supported hooks and event conventions.

sections.title: Test your content
sections.text: Preview scenes and inspect the media runtime while developing your game.

sections.title: Import videos and build your scenes
sections.text: Upload video clips, images and other media to your library, then use them in scenes for your backglass or other displays. Combine video with text and images to create attract sequences, animations and gameplay screens.

sections.title: Show live scores and game information
sections.text: Text doesn't have to stay the same throughout a game. Use supported live values to show scores, player information and other changing details on your displays. Update the content as the game progresses without rebuilding the scene.

sections.title: Build interactive backglass displays
sections.text: Pinball CTL supports Godot scene packs, so you can create animated menus, score displays and interactive screens. Map supported cabinet inputs to scene controls, letting players move through menus and make selections using the machine's buttons.

sections.title: Connect your Godot scenes to the game
sections.text: Godot scenes can receive updated text values from Pinball CTL and send supported custom events back to the Rules system. That means your display can respond to gameplay and your menus can trigger actions in the wider game.
sections.after_text: The integration uses supported input mappings and runtime hooks. Not every Godot project will work unchanged, so custom scenes should be tested before use in a cabinet.

sections.title: See how it works
sections.text: For example, a player could use the flipper buttons to navigate a menu on the backglass. During play, the display could update the score and show an imported video when a rule triggers a media scene.

steps.title: Layer
steps.text: Add the visual elements and adjust them on the stage.

steps.title: Shape
steps.text: Set timing, priority and interruption behaviour for the scene.

steps.title: Present
steps.text: Choose the target display and validate playback on the machine.

example.title: A score display with its own identity
example.text: Combine an image background with live text and a custom font, then use scene policies to control how it appears alongside other game content.

live-view.headline: Keep the whole response in view.
live-view.body: Live View brings the visual playfield and runtime tools together. It is a place to explore configured inputs and observe the relationship between rules, lights and media while developing the machine.

sections.title: Test playfield inputs
sections.text: Use the stage preview and keyboard or mouse controls to trigger configured inputs.

sections.title: Try lighting and media
sections.text: Preview lighting scenes and launch supported media scenes from the same testing page.

sections.title: Work before your cabinet is finished
sections.text: Develop and preview without a complete machine. Connected event-path testing and physical outputs still require real hardware.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.text: Build a layout and configure the inputs you want to exercise.

steps.title: Observe
steps.text: Follow how a test input changes the visual playfield.

steps.title: Investigate
steps.text: Use the relevant authoring or diagnostic module to refine the behaviour.

example.title: Keyboard testing can reach real hardware
example.text: With an ESP connected, simulated inputs use the bridge and firmware event path. Treat configured output actions with the same care as a physical button press.

playfield-layout.headline: Make the machine recognisable on screen.
playfield-layout.body: Place your components on a visual stage and tune their appearance to reflect the playfield. A useful layout becomes shared context for editing, lighting and Live View.

sections.title: Arrange the playfield
sections.text: Place and customise components on the visual stage.

sections.title: Set up input controls
sections.text: Assign keyboard bindings to components for development and testing.

sections.title: Test responses
sections.text: Use the layout's event-testing tools to check configured interactions.

steps.title: Arrange
steps.text: Position the components to match your machine.

steps.title: Describe
steps.text: Adjust shape, size, rotation and appearance.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: Bring the layout into Live View and lighting development.

example.title: Design before the cabinet is complete
example.text: You can develop the visual organisation while the physical build evolves, then refine bindings and positions as hardware is connected.

dashboard.headline: A first check before the next change.
dashboard.body: The dashboard collects status from the host and controller into one overview. Use it to establish whether the machine is connected and ready for the more focused work that follows.

sections.title: Check the essentials
sections.text: See controller connectivity, runtime services and machine status together.

sections.title: Spot what needs attention
sections.text: Use the overview to identify a connection or service that needs checking.

sections.title: Open the right tool
sections.text: Move from the dashboard to the relevant configuration or diagnostic module.

steps.title: Scan
steps.text: Check connectivity and the services you rely on.

steps.title: Choose
steps.text: Open the tool for the part of the machine you are working on.

steps.title: Recheck
steps.text: Return after a deployment or maintenance task to verify the state.

example.title: Before a test session
example.text: A quick look at the controller, bridge and dependency state helps catch a disconnected device before you start changing rules to solve the wrong problem.

performance.headline: Measure waiting time, not just event counts.
performance.body: Throughput is useful, but responsiveness also depends on how long work waits. Performance puts event rates, queued work and confirmation latency together so you can read a busy period in context.

sections.title: See event rates
sections.text: Compare incoming events, host processing and ESP confirmations over time.

sections.title: Find slowdowns
sections.text: Inspect queue depth, the oldest waiting event and delivery latency.

sections.title: Understand overloads
sections.text: Review protective stop and recovery information before resetting or testing again.

sections.title: Investigate the system as a connected whole.
sections.text: A delayed effect might involve a queue, a disconnected controller or a host-side consumer. Combine performance history, event logs and connection status to narrow down where the behaviour changes.

sections.title: Follow events through the system
sections.text: See how events pass through the bridge, host and ESP confirmation path.

sections.title: Understand safety stops
sections.text: See overload and recovery information alongside the tools used to investigate the cause.

sections.title: Different rates can be normal
sections.text: Incoming events, host-processed work and ESP confirmations describe different parts of the system. A host-only scoring or sound event need not produce a matching ESP transmission.

steps.title: Establish
steps.text: Watch ordinary gameplay to learn its normal activity pattern.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: Look for sustained backlog and a widening delivery-time gap.

steps.title: Investigate
steps.text: Use the related logs and configuration to explain the change.

example.title: A confirmation is not physical feedback
example.text: An ESP confirmation means an event was accepted. It does not prove a coil moved, and it does not measure the immediate local response of an ESP-owned switch rule.

event-logs.headline: Find the useful detail in a busy machine.
event-logs.body: View web, bridge, ESP and event output from the browser. Switch perspective and filter the visible messages when you need to follow a specific component or moment.

sections.title: Choose a log source
sections.text: Switch between web, bridge, ESP and event logs.

sections.title: Filter the output
sections.text: Narrow the visible messages to the activity you need to investigate.

sections.title: Trace a problem
sections.text: Use logged events and service messages to understand how your machine responded.

steps.title: Select
steps.text: Choose the source closest to the symptom.

steps.title: Focus
steps.text: Filter for the relevant event, device or error.

steps.title: Inspect
steps.text: Open a structured entry and follow its fields into your configuration.

example.title: A sound fires twice
example.text: Compare the event stream and the configured consumers to see whether two inputs arrived or one input triggered two actions. The log gives you evidence for the next change.

service-log.headline: Remember the work done on the physical machine.
service-log.body: Runtime logs explain software activity. The service log records maintenance: what was changed, who did the work and what should happen next.

sections.title: Record maintenance
sections.text: Keep notes about cleaning, adjustments, repairs and replaced components.
items: Service, repair, recall and warranty categories

sections.title: Keep a history
sections.text: Record service dates and types so you can see what work has been done.

sections.title: Find previous work
sections.text: Filter entries to revisit earlier repairs and maintenance.

steps.title: Record
steps.text: Add the task and the person carrying it out.

steps.title: Explain
steps.text: Describe the parts, outcome and any remaining work.

steps.title: Revisit
steps.text: Search the service history before repeating a repair.

example.title: A coil replacement with context
example.text: Record the part fitted and the test result, then attach the relevant photo or document. The next inspection starts with more than a date and a guess.

integrity-check.headline: Find the references left behind as a game evolves.
integrity-check.body: Deleting or renaming one element can affect another. Integrity Check brings cross-module references into view so cleanup is guided by what the project actually uses.

sections.title: Check dependencies
sections.text: Audit references between hardware, rules, layout, lighting, audio and scoring.

sections.title: Find unused or broken items
sections.text: Review missing links and orphaned configuration entries.

sections.title: Resolve carefully
sections.text: Inspect findings before using supported resolution tools; review changes before syncing.

steps.title: Scan
steps.text: Run the reference check for the current project.

steps.title: Review
steps.text: Distinguish unused items from genuinely broken links.

steps.title: Resolve
steps.text: Apply appropriate fixes deliberately, then review the updated report.

example.title: Unused does not always mean unwanted
example.text: An asset can be prepared for a future mode without being referenced yet. The report provides context; you decide whether it belongs in the project.

settings.headline: Keep installation choices separate from game logic.
settings.body: Project identity, access, firmware sources and reporting preferences belong in a central place. Settings groups those choices so they remain discoverable as the project grows.

sections.title: Configure your installation
sections.text: Manage project identity and installation-wide preferences.

sections.title: Export your project
sections.text: Create an export of supported project data for transfer or backup.
items: Import and export tools package instance data for transfer. Review the destination before importing: the operation can overwrite existing project files.

sections.title: Import project data
sections.text: Use the import workflow to bring supported project data into an installation.

steps.title: Personalise
steps.text: Set the project identity and relevant installation preferences.

steps.title: Review
steps.text: Check access, reporting and firmware-source settings.

steps.title: Transfer
steps.text: Use an export when preparing a project move or backup.

example.title: Moving from the development host
example.text: A project bundle helps carry authored data into another installation. Host-specific devices, paths and runtime dependencies still need checking on the destination.

wifi.headline: Keep the host reachable from your workspace.
wifi.body: Check the network name, IP address and connection state in one view. On supported platforms, the same module provides a place to update Wi-Fi credentials.

sections.title: Check connection details
sections.text: View the current network name, address and connection status.

sections.title: Update Wi-Fi settings
sections.text: Enter supported network credentials from the browser on compatible platforms.

sections.title: Confirm connectivity
sections.text: Check the new connection after changing networks; some functions depend on host platform support.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: Review the current host network information.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.text: Confirm the intended network before applying a change.

steps.title: Reconnect
steps.text: Use the host’s new address if the network change moves it.

example.title: A different network can mean a different address
example.text: When moving a cabinet, your existing browser bookmark may no longer reach the Pi. Confirm the new network and address before investigating application services.
